titre: Skansen Reports Itself, and British Law Convicts It Anyway
accroche: In 2018, a London company that reported its own internal bribery is found guilty all the same: the law judges only what came before the facts.
contenu_vulgarise:
In January 2014, a new chief executive takes up his post at Skansen Interiors, a London office fit-out company with about thirty employees. He becomes concerned about payments made to a project manager at DTZ, who helped the company win two office refurbishment contracts in 2013, worth about six million pounds in total. He opens an internal investigation and puts in place an anti-bribery policy, the company having had none until then. The former managing director still tries to make one last payment, of about £29,000: it is stopped, and he is fired. The company then reports itself to the police and the National Crime Agency. Four years later, in 2018, a London court finds Skansen Interiors guilty all the same of breaching the British anti-bribery law.

## The only way to defend yourself

The Bribery Act 2010, enacted on April 8, 2010 and in force on July 1, 2011 after a delay meant to let the Ministry of Justice publish its guidance, creates in section 7 an offense specific to companies. An organization commits an offense as soon as a person acting on its behalf pays a bribe for the benefit of its business, whether or not its managers knew of it. The law provides only one defense, set out in subsection 2 of the same section: it is up to the company to prove that it had “adequate procedures” in place designed to prevent such conduct. The burden of proof is on the company, not on the prosecution to show the contrary.

At Skansen's trial, the jury did not have to judge the quality of the company's reaction in 2014: it had reported the facts, fired the wrongdoer, and cooperated fully with the police. The question posed by the law concerns another, earlier moment, that of 2013, when the contracts were won: did adequate procedures already exist at the time? The jury found that they did not. Skansen Interiors is the first company to rely on the section 7(2) defense, and the jury rejects it. With no business activity and no assets, the company receives only an absolute discharge, but the guilty verdict is a landmark.

## The shift

The case shifts the very meaning of anti-bribery compliance: it is not a file one completes after being caught. It is a state of affairs one must be able to prove beforehand. A company that is beyond reproach in its reaction can remain guilty of its past. The British choice contrasts with the French Sapin II law of 2016, which requires certain large companies to run an eight-measure anti-corruption program (a code of conduct, an internal whistleblowing system, risk mapping, training, internal controls, among others). The French Anti-Corruption Agency checks its existence, quality, and effectiveness before any offense and independently of any prosecution. Two countries, two ways of placing the requirement: in the United Kingdom, it is judged at trial, as a defense the company must prove; in France, it is checked upstream, before any suspicion even arises.

repere.texte: The Bribery Act 2010 (United Kingdom) came into force on July 1, 2011. In 2018, Skansen Interiors Limited is the first company to rely on the “adequate procedures” defense of its section 7, subsection 2, and the jury rejects it, despite its voluntary self-reporting of the facts.
repere.source: UK Government, Bribery Act 2010, section 7 (legislation.gov.uk); Addleshaw Goddard, R v Skansen Interiors Limited, Case Summary, April 2018

carte.punch: It reported itself. British law convicted it anyway.
carte.idee: In 2018, Skansen Interiors is found guilty of bribery even though it had itself alerted the police after discovering the facts. British law does not judge the quality of the reaction after the fact: it demands procedures already in place beforehand.
carte.source_courte: Bribery Act 2010, s. 7; R v Skansen Interiors, 2018

quiz.question: Why was Skansen Interiors convicted in 2018 despite its voluntary report to the authorities?
choix: Because British law recognizes no defense for companies prosecuted for bribery
Because the legal defense concerns the procedures in place before the facts, not the quality of the reaction once the bribery is discovered
Because the court found its cooperation with the police insufficient
Because the law imposes an automatic fine as soon as a bribe is proven, whatever the company's reaction
quiz.explication: The only defense provided by section 7 concerns the adequate procedures in place at the time of the facts, before the new chief executive arrived; a voluntary report in 2014, however complete, cannot make up for their earlier absence.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was the approximate total value of the two contracts won thanks to the bribes?
choix: About six million pounds, for two office refurbishment contracts at DTZ
About twenty-nine thousand pounds, for a separate legal consulting contract
About two hundred thousand pounds, for an industrial cleaning contract
About six hundred thousand pounds, for an IT maintenance contract
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The new chief executive becomes concerned about payments tied to two office refurbishment contracts won in 2013 at DTZ, worth about six million pounds in total.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who bears the burden of proof for the “adequate procedures” defense of section 7?
choix: The court, which must establish on its own that adequate procedures existed
The prosecution, which must prove the absence of adequate procedures at the company
The company itself, which must prove that it had adequate procedures in place
The Ministry of Justice, which audits procedures before any trial
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 7, subsection 2, sets out a single defense whose proof falls on the prosecuted company, not on the prosecution, which reverses the usual burden.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What penalty did Skansen Interiors ultimately receive despite the guilty verdict?
choix: A fine equal to the total amount of the bribes paid
An absolute discharge, for lack of business activity and assets
A permanent ban on operating in the construction sector
A two-year probation sentence imposed on its managers
quiz_supplementaire.explication: With no business activity and no assets, the company receives only an absolute discharge, but the guilty verdict is a landmark for companies covered by section 7.
